questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of organic growth?
options: Growth generated from within the business, by selling more, adding products or entering new markets
Growth achieved by acquiring another business
Growth funded entirely by borrowing
Growth in the size of the whole industry
questions.why: Organic growth is built rather than bought. It is slower, cheaper and lower risk than acquiring another business.
whyNot: That is inorganic growth.
How it is funded does not define it; organic growth is often funded from retained profit.
That is market growth.

questions.stem: What is usually the main source of finance for organic growth?
options: Retained profit
A hostile takeover
Issuing shares to the public
Venture capital
questions.why: Retained profit needs no interest and dilutes no ownership, which is why organic growth and profitability are linked: an unprofitable business has nothing to reinvest.
whyNot: That is a method of inorganic growth.
Possible, and usually associated with larger or faster growth.
Usually associated with high-growth or inorganic strategies.

questions.stem: What is the main disadvantage of organic growth?
options: It is slow, so competitors can acquire their way to scale faster
It dilutes the owner's control
It always requires large borrowing
It damages the business culture
questions.why: Speed is the real trade-off. In a fast-growing market, slow growth means losing share, and slow can be fatal.
whyNot: Organic growth is precisely what preserves control.
It can often be funded from profits.
It preserves culture; acquisitions are what disrupt it.

questions.stem: Why does organic growth preserve the business culture?
options: There is no second workforce with different ways of working to integrate
Organic growth requires no new staff
Culture cannot change in a growing business
Organic growth is always slow enough to ignore culture
questions.why: Culture clash is the most common cause of acquisition failure. Growing from within means new staff join an existing culture rather than two cultures colliding.
whyNot: It usually involves recruiting; they join an established culture.
Culture does evolve with growth, which is the diseconomy of motivation.
Pace helps, and the substantive reason is that there is no second culture.

questions.stem: Besides cash, what else limits the pace of organic growth?
options: Management capacity to absorb the change
The colour of the branding
The number of competitors
The legal form of the business
questions.why: A business can only grow as fast as its management can manage. This is the entrepreneur-to-leader constraint from WBS11 topic 1.3.4.5, and it is frequently the binding limit rather than money.
whyNot: Irrelevant.
Competitors affect the need for speed, not the internal capacity.
Legal form affects finance options, not management capacity.

questions.stem: Why is franchising an attractive route to organic growth for a franchisor?
options: It expands the brand using franchisees' capital while the franchisor keeps control of the model
It requires no brand or business model
It guarantees consistent standards everywhere
It is a form of inorganic growth
questions.why: The franchisor grows fast without funding each outlet. The cost is reliance on franchisees to maintain standards, because reputational damage from one outlet affects the whole brand.
whyNot: Both are exactly what the franchisee is paying for.
Maintaining standards across franchisees is the main difficulty.
For the franchisor it expands the existing brand, so it is organic.

questions.stem: What is the opportunity cost of funding organic growth from retained profit?
options: The profit is not available as a cash buffer or as a payment to owners
There is no opportunity cost, because retained profit is free
The business must pay interest on it
Ownership is diluted
questions.why: A business that reinvests everything is growing and fragile: there is nothing held back for a bad month. Naming that trade-off is straightforward evaluation.
whyNot: It carries no interest and a real opportunity cost.
No interest is payable on the business's own money.
No new shareholders are involved.
